newsitem.title: GERMANY: Recovery reduces German rate cut hopes, banks say.
newsitem.headline: Recovery reduces German rate cut hopes, banks say.

text.p: Chances of further German interest rate cuts have fallen as economic recovery gathers pace, but with inflation subdued a rate hike can be ruled out until late next year, the German BdB banking association said on Thursday.
Germany's economy bottomed out last winter and is enjoying an export-led recovery -- helped by an easing in the mark's exchange rate and moderate wage increases.

Most growth forecasts for this year have been revised up by economists to one percent -- a forecast "well underpinned" by developments but still below the long-term trend, the BdB said in its October monthly report.
"Money market rates have reached a very low level. A further cut in leading interest rates cannot be excluded under certain conditions, but is rather unlikely," the report said.
"On the other hand, solid price stability and lack of inflationary dangers mean that a step on the monetary policy brakes will not be on the agenda until far into next year."

Germany's repo rate was last cut to three percent at the end of August, and market expectations of further cuts have subsided even though the Bundesbank has tried not to completely extinguish them, the BdB said.
Chances of a turnaround in the falling trend of German bond yields are also slim, with the influential U.S. bond market still calm about inflation after four years of economic growth.
Germany's economy grew in the second quarter by 1.5 percent against the weather-hit first quarter, but signs are mounting that there was an acceleration in the third quarter.

Industrial production in July and August grew by two percent compared to the previous two months, with improved orders feeding through into output. However, manufacturing growth was more modest and recovery in east Germany is lagging.
But, despite the economic recovery, there is little sign of any impact on unemployment, which at near four million in September was 300,000 up on a year earlier.
"An end to job losses cannot be expected this year -- for an improvement economic growth is still too slow and the labour market is in any case a lagging indicator," the report said.
